<reason>A won a competitive debate by keeping the motion as a burden-of-proof rule under uncertainty and making the error-cost comparison easier to vote: crisis leverage is costly and sticky, a blocked bid is at least theoretically reversible. B’s “metal that ships” case was punchy and often sharper on capital scarcity and host licenses, but never fully escaped the tension between “title does not control ore” and “losing the rival-tied bidder kills the mine.” A’s answers on mitigation versus a ban, plus the hard-case hostage-supply weighing, gave the cleaner reason to adopt the presumption. A clipped Rebuttal 1 was a real execution cost and kept this from being a larger win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s Rebuttal 2 fork: if ownership is geopolitically irrelevant the block is cheap, but if losing the bidder stalls the project then title is a real lever—the same reason state acquirers pay premiums. B’s “finances the pit without redirecting licensed ore” reply was the best counter, yet did not collapse the contradiction.</best_rebuttal>
